item.title: Stable deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes with reduced efficiency roll-off via accelerated exciton utilization
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02029-4 Deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes leveraging phosphor-assisted TADF-sensitized fluorescence enable accelerated exciton dynamics, resulting in devices with an external quantum efficiency of 35.9% and an LT80 lifetime of 632 h.

item.title: Delaying light from quantum dots
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02015-w Förster energy transfer can prolong the photoluminescence decay of a receiving colloidal quantum dot, revealing a possible route to optically control recombination in nanocrystal assemblies.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
item.description: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions.

item.title: New stability rules distinguish quantum phases of matter that an older method wrongly groups together
item.description: Most of us recognize basic phases of matter and their properties: solids maintain their shape, liquids flow freely with constant volume, and gases expand to fill their container. Quantum phases, on the other hand, are much harder to categorize, overturning traditional notions of what a phase even is and forcing physicists to rethink their definitions.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computer observes foundational quantum effect in a new setting
item.description: Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

item.title: Light reads electron spins inside porous crystals, opening path to quantum chemical sensors
item.description: University of Glasgow researchers are part of an international collaboration that could lead to a new generation of quantum sensors. The team, which included researchers from the University of Tokyo, University of Glasgow, University of Sheffield and Kobe University, has for the first time used light to read out the magnetic spin of electrons trapped inside a porous crystalline material known as a metal-organic framework (MOF).

item.title: Gravity and light reveal how liquids turn into thin fibers
item.description: From spiders spinning their webs to the manufacturing of textiles, the formation of fibers from liquids plays an important role in both nature and industry. Yet accurately predicting the properties of such fibers remains a challenge. The fiber is often much thinner than the nozzle from which a polymer or solution is extruded. Factors such as temperature, flow conditions and chemical reactions ultimately determine a fiber's thickness and strength.

item.title: Levitating glass sphere becomes entangled with light at room temperature
item.description: Today, many physicists are actively exploring how light could be used to link objects through quantum entanglement. By fully harnessing the effect, they hope to unlock a wide array of applications, from secure communication networks spanning vast distances to sensitive new tests of the fundamental laws of physics.

item.description: A cryostat that can reach temperatures of 4 K and warm back up again within just two hours offers an efficient solution for testing the electronic components needed to build quantum computers The post Faster cryogenics speeds up quantum testing appeared first on Physics World .

item.title: Ultrafast core-level spectroscopy reveals elusive precursors of exciton condensation in quantum materials
item.description: Many fascinating phases in quantum materials emerge when electrons, atoms and other microscopic components begin to act collectively. But these phases do not necessarily appear out of nowhere when a material crosses a transition temperature. Before long-range order develops, microscopic fluctuations can already be present.

item.title: Superconducting circuit links smaller photon groups into larger entangled states
item.description: Quantum computers, computer systems that leverage the laws of quantum mechanics, store and process information using qubits (i.e., quantum bits). In many quantum computers, qubits are linked via entanglement, a quantum mechanical effect that connects particles in such a way that their shared state cannot be described as separate, independent states.

item.title: How researchers tell different quantum excitations apart in individual molecules
item.description: Molecules can be placed in a wide variety of quantum states. How can these states be distinguished in measurements when theoretical models are unreliable? Which excitation process lies behind which measurement signal?

item.title: One quantum material, two superconducting states: Stretching helps explain conflicting experiments
item.description: Unconventional superconductors can host unusual electronic states, but understanding what drives their superconductivity becomes difficult when different forms of order coexist. The kagome metal CsV3Sb5 has become a particularly debated example.

item.title: Real-number quantum theory can be more wrong than you thought
item.description: Imaginary numbers first appeared in the 16th century as a mathematical invention, introduced to solve equations that real numbers could not. As the name implies, many treated them as kind of trick to get results, rather than an underlying truth about the nature of reality. Although highly controversial at the time, these numbers are now ubiquitous […] The post Real-number quantum theory can be more wrong than you thought appeared first on Physics World .

item.title: Phase control of interfering stimulated Raman pathways in the XUV regime
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02024-9 Researchers modulate population transfer from the helium ground state to a metastable state by controlling the relative phase between two interfering stimulated Raman pathways through the continuum, demonstrating phase-coherent control in the extreme ultraviolet.

item.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
item.description: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity.

Nature Photonics spoke with Zhentang Zhao, director of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility and the SHINE project, about the facility’s capabilities and future plans.

item.title: Time-stretch spectroscopy breaks temporal aliasing barrier
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02006-x A temporally super-resolved single-shot method overcomes the long-standing temporal–spectral trade-off in time-stretch spectroscopy. The outcome is continuous measurements of non-repetitive spectral dynamics with picosecond resolution, providing a three-orders-of-magnitude improvement over the current state of the art.
